newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela quake toll rises as search continues.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela quake toll rises as search continues.

text.p: Search teams in eastern Venezuela redoubled efforts on Friday to find any survivors still trapped in rubble from a quake that destroyed buildings, buried children in their classrooms and killed at least 68 people.
Early Friday morning firemen fed 50-foot (15-metre) air hoses down holes opened in the rubble.

"We've injected air to help anybody still alive to keep going," fire chief Angel Freites said. "That's our hope. We can't guarantee it 100 percent but every rescuer's dream is to find someone alive, but it's not a certainty."
The quake, measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale, struck Wednesday afternoon, sending schools, houses and office buildings crashing to the ground.

"Up to now we have recovered 22 bodies from the building. This brings the official death toll to 68," Civil Defence director Francisco Espin told Reuters as he supervised rescuers at the ruins of an office building in Sucre state capital Cumana.
Espin said eight more bodies had been located within the twisted metal and concrete of the once six-story building and said the death toll could rise.
State Governor Ramon Martinez said 469 people were injured in the quake -- Venezuela's worst for three decades -- and 48 people were pulled alive from wrecked buildings.
The majority of the deaths occurred in the small agricultural town Cariaco, 40 miles (64 km) east of Cumana, where a high school and nursery school fell on pupils and teachers.
At least 41 bodies were recovered from the fallen masonry and scattered exercise books. Two-year-old infants and an 81-year old man were among the dead.
For many of the children, Thursday was to have been the last day of classes before the summer break.

Fear that the tragedy at the Raimundo Martinez Centeno high school in Cariaco was far worse eased slightly late on Thursday when rescuers uncovered an empty classroom thought to contain up to 100 bodies. The pupils had managed to scramble to safety through a tiny gap in the ruins left after the roof crashed onto their desks, rescuers said.

Cariaco, a tiny town of 13,000, bore the brunt of the quake, which devastated three quarters of its buildings. Residents spent their second night on Thursday sleeping on plastic sheets in the debris-strewn streets and in the local sports stadium. Local authorities declared a curfew.
Along the small villages that lined the recently re-opened highway between Cumana and Cariaco, survivors lit candles and spent the night sitting on plastic chairs in improvised shelters.
Mothers sobbed as President Rafael Caldera paid a brief visit to the area on Thursday. "Our houses are ruined, our children dead," said one woman.
Caldera declared three days of national mourning.
The French embassy confirmed that one French citizen was killed by the quake. There were no other reports of foreigners among the dead or injured.
Urban Development Minister Julio Marti said very early estimates put infrastructural damage at $8 million.
The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck at 3:25 pm EDT (1925 GMT) on Wednesday. FUNVISIS said the epicentre was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast.
More than 30 aftershocks have been recorded since the first tremor, causing considerable alarm but no further damage.
The 1967 quake killed about 300 in the Venezuela capital and surrounding areas, FUNVISIS said.
